analogy.p: The muscles are the kitchen and suddenly a huge number of orders arrive (exercise). The heart and lungs are the delivery lorries and the waiters: they speed up to bring ingredients (oxygen and glucose) and take rubbish (carbon dioxide) away. If ingredients cannot arrive fast enough, the chefs use a quick but messy shortcut that makes waste (lactic acid) and little food. After the rush, the cleaners (liver, using extra oxygen) tidy up the mess, which is the oxygen debt. It breaks down because the kitchen cannot turn its waste back into ingredients the way the liver converts lactic acid into glucose.

bullets: **Exercise = muscles contracting more**, so they need more **energy** from respiration.
The body responds by **delivering more oxygen and glucose** to muscles and **removing more carbon dioxide**.
If oxygen delivery cannot keep up, muscles switch to **anaerobic respiration**, producing **lactic acid**.
After exercise the body repays an **oxygen debt** to deal with the lactic acid.
Higher and Foundation papers both test this; typical marks are 2 to 6.
Always give the **reason** for a change (WHY), not just the change itself.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.4.2 'Response to exercise' asks you to describe how the body changes during exercise and why. You must know that **heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase**, that muscles can store **glycogen** which is converted to glucose, and what happens when there is **insufficient oxygen** (**anaerobic respiration**, **lactic acid**, **muscle fatigue**, **oxygen debt**). Questions mix recall, explanation and data interpretation, so you must be able to link each change to its cause.

bullets: Energy from respiration is used for **muscle contraction** (contractile proteins sliding past each other).
**Respiration is the process that transfers energy from glucose**; it is **exothermic**, so exercise also makes you warmer.
More respiration means a faster demand for **oxygen and glucose** and faster production of **carbon dioxide**.
Glucose and oxygen reach muscles through the **blood**, pumped by the heart.
Carbon dioxide is carried by the blood back to the **lungs** to be breathed out.
The delivery system (heart and lungs) must therefore speed up during exercise.
core.h: Why exercising muscles need more energy
core.p: Muscle contraction is an active process that uses energy released by **respiration** in the cells. The harder you exercise, the more muscle fibres contract and the faster they contract, so the **rate of respiration** in muscle cells increases. Respiration needs **glucose** and **oxygen** (aerobic) and produces **carbon dioxide** as a waste product. Therefore more glucose and oxygen must be supplied and more carbon dioxide removed.

bullets: Word equation: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water**.
Symbol equation: **C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O**.
It is **complete oxidation** of glucose, so the maximum energy is released.
Takes place in **mitochondria** (most of the stages).
Is the main process during **moderate, sustained exercise** such as jogging.
Produces CO2, which is why **breathing rate rises** (more CO2 to remove).
Compare: the same equation is used for all aerobic respiration in plants and animals.
core.h: Aerobic respiration: the equation to know
core.p: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose completely. It happens in the **mitochondria** of cells and releases the most energy per glucose molecule. When oxygen supply is good, muscles use this route. You must be able to write the equation in words and in symbols.

bullets: Resting heart rate is typically about **60 to 80 beats per minute**; during hard exercise it can exceed **150 beats per minute**.
More blood per minute reaches the muscles, so more **oxygen and glucose** are delivered.
**Carbon dioxide** is removed faster, preventing a build-up.
Blood vessels to muscles **widen (vasodilate)** so more blood flows through them.
Fitter people have a lower resting heart rate and recover faster.
Heart rate can be measured by **pulse** at the wrist or neck, or with a heart rate monitor.
Link: the heart is a double pump (see Heart, blood vessels and blood).
core.p: During exercise your **heart rate increases**, so the heart pumps blood around the body faster. Faster blood flow delivers **oxygen and glucose** to the muscles more quickly and carries away **carbon dioxide** (and heat) more quickly. This keeps aerobic respiration going for longer. Heart rate is controlled automatically by the brain responding to rising carbon dioxide and by hormones such as adrenaline.

bullets: **Breathing rate** = number of breaths per minute (about 12 to 15 at rest).
**Breath volume** = volume of air taken in per breath; deeper breaths increase it.
Faster, deeper breathing keeps the **concentration gradient** of oxygen and carbon dioxide steep in the alveoli.
More **oxygen** enters the blood to be delivered to the muscles.
More **carbon dioxide** leaves the blood to be breathed out.
Intercostal muscles and the diaphragm contract more strongly and more often.
Breathing rate stays high after exercise to repay the oxygen debt.
core.h: Increased breathing rate and breath volume
core.p: Breathing rate (breaths per minute) and **breath volume** (the volume of air in each breath, also called tidal volume) both increase during exercise. This increases the volume of air moving in and out of the lungs each minute, so more oxygen **diffuses** into the blood and more carbon dioxide diffuses out. The steeper concentration gradients at the alveoli make gas exchange faster.

bullets: Glycogen is a **storage carbohydrate** made of many glucose molecules.
Stored in **muscle cells** and the **liver**.
Converted to **glucose** when exercising, so respiration can continue.
The hormone **glucagon** triggers glycogen breakdown in the liver (link to homeostasis); adrenaline also promotes it.
Athletes may eat carbohydrate-rich food to build up glycogen stores before events.
Without enough glucose, muscles cannot keep respiring, which leads to fatigue.
core.p: Muscles contain a store of **glycogen**, a large polymer of glucose. During exercise, glycogen is **converted back to glucose**, which is then used in respiration to supply extra energy quickly without waiting for glucose from the blood. Glycogen is also stored in the **liver**. Once glycogen stores run out, the muscles tire and performance falls.

bullets: Word equation: **glucose → lactic acid**.
It is **incomplete oxidation** of glucose, so it releases **much less energy** than aerobic respiration.
It happens in the **cytoplasm**, not the mitochondria.
It provides a quick burst of energy when oxygen supply is limited (e.g. sprinting).
No carbon dioxide is produced in animal anaerobic respiration, so it does not itself raise breathing rate.
Compare yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide (fermentation).
core.h: Anaerobic respiration when oxygen is insufficient
core.p: During vigorous exercise the blood cannot supply oxygen as fast as the muscles use it. The muscles then also respire **anaerobically**, which is respiration **without oxygen**. Glucose is only **partially broken down**, so far less energy is released per glucose molecule, but the energy is released quickly. In animals the product is **lactic acid**, not carbon dioxide and water.

bullets: Lactic acid accumulates when anaerobic respiration is occurring.
**Muscle fatigue** = muscles become tired and stop contracting efficiently.
Lactic acid lowers pH in the muscle, which interferes with enzyme and contraction function.
It must be removed by the blood and processed by the liver.
Fitter people can exercise longer before fatigue because they supply oxygen better.
A person may feel pain or cramp as lactic acid builds.
core.p: Lactic acid builds up in muscles if it is made faster than it is removed. A high concentration of lactic acid is linked to **muscle fatigue**, where the muscles stop contracting efficiently, and to cramp-like pain. Blood passing through the muscles carries lactic acid away, but during intense exercise this cannot keep pace. Muscle fatigue is the reason you eventually have to stop or slow down.

bullets: **Oxygen debt** = extra oxygen needed to react with lactic acid and remove it.
Explains why **breathing rate and heart rate stay high** after stopping.
The oxygen is used to oxidise lactic acid, producing **carbon dioxide and water**, mostly in the liver.
Bigger oxygen debt means a longer recovery period.
Recovery time is a measure of fitness: fitter people recover faster.
Oxygen also helps replenish oxygen stores in muscle and restore glycogen.
core.p: After vigorous exercise you keep breathing deeply and your heart rate stays high for a while. This is because you need extra oxygen to deal with the lactic acid built up in the muscles. The AQA definition is: the **oxygen debt** is the **amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells**. Once the lactic acid has been dealt with, breathing and heart rate return to normal.

bullets: Lactic acid is carried in the **blood plasma** from muscle to **liver**.
In the liver it is **converted back to glucose**.
Glucose is then reused or stored as **glycogen**.
This is why the heart must keep pumping fast after exercise: to keep lactic acid moving.
Part of the lactic acid is also oxidised to release energy.
The cycle means no glucose is wasted.
core.h: Removing lactic acid: the role of blood and liver
core.p: Lactic acid cannot stay in the muscle. **Blood flowing through the muscles transports lactic acid to the liver**, where it is **converted back into glucose**. This conversion requires energy and oxygen, which is exactly what the oxygen debt supplies. The glucose can be released into the blood or stored as glycogen again.

bullets: **Oxygen**: aerobic needs it; anaerobic does not.
**Products**: aerobic gives carbon dioxide + water; anaerobic (animals) gives lactic acid.
**Energy**: aerobic releases a lot per glucose molecule; anaerobic releases much less.
**Glucose breakdown**: aerobic is complete; anaerobic is incomplete.
**Where**: aerobic mostly in mitochondria; anaerobic in cytoplasm.
**Speed**: anaerobic can supply energy quickly in short bursts.
**Duration**: aerobic can continue for long periods; anaerobic is limited by fatigue and oxygen debt.
core.p: Examiners love comparison questions. Make sure you use comparative words: more, less, faster, slower. Aerobic respiration releases far more energy but needs oxygen; anaerobic is quick but inefficient and produces harmful lactic acid.

bullets: **Independent variable**: type or intensity of exercise (or time); **dependent variable**: pulse or breathing rate.
**Control variables**: same person, same exercise duration, same time of day, same method of counting pulse.
Count pulse for a full **minute** or for 15 s and multiply by 4 for beats per minute.
Repeat and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability.
**Recovery time** = time taken to return to resting rate.
Percentage increase = (increase ÷ original) × 100.
Compare fit and unfit people: fitter person has lower resting rate and faster recovery.
core.h: Data skills: investigating the effect of exercise
core.p: A common practical is measuring pulse rate (or breathing rate) at rest, during exercise and during recovery. Graphs usually show heart rate against time: a flat line at rest, a rise when exercise starts, a plateau, and then a gradual fall during recovery. You may be asked to calculate a percentage increase or the recovery time.

bullets: **Respiration (4.4.1)**: aerobic and anaerobic equations underpin everything here.
**Heart and circulatory system (4.2)**: heart pumps blood faster to deliver oxygen and glucose.
**Gas exchange (4.2/4.3)**: diffusion across alveoli depends on concentration gradients.
**Homeostasis (4.5)**: glucagon and glycogen regulate blood glucose; the body also controls temperature during exercise.
**Metabolism (4.4.3)**: the liver converts lactic acid back to glucose.
Higher: explain that anaerobic respiration is a short-term solution because lactic acid builds up and the debt must be repaid.
Higher: evaluate training: regular exercise increases heart size, muscle mass and capillaries, improving oxygen supply.
core.h: Link to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: This topic connects to many others, which is how harder questions are built. Higher-tier answers are expected to link several ideas, for example explaining why an athlete continues to breathe heavily after finishing a race.

exam: **State/Name** (1 mark): short recall, e.g. 'Name the product of anaerobic respiration in muscles' → lactic acid.
**Describe** (2 to 3 marks): give the changes only, e.g. heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume all increase.
**Explain** (2 to 4 marks): every change needs 'because' or 'so that' linked to oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide or energy.
Use the model phrase: **'to supply more oxygen and glucose to the muscles for aerobic respiration'**.
For oxygen debt always say: **'extra oxygen needed to react with lactic acid'**.
4 mark compare questions: give at least two differences with comparative words (more, less, faster).

6 mark question structure: (1) muscles contract, need energy; (2) heart/breathing changes with reasons; (3) anaerobic respiration; (4) lactic acid and fatigue; (5) oxygen debt; (6) lactic acid to liver.
Graph questions: quote **values with units** from the graph (e.g. 'increased from 70 to 150 beats per minute').
Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100; show working for method marks.
Do not write 'anaerobic respiration is respiration without air' only; say **'without oxygen'**.
Check the equation: **glucose → lactic acid** has no oxygen on the left.

mistakes.r: In animals it produces only lactic acid (glucose → lactic acid).
mistakes.w: Anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid and carbon dioxide.

mistakes.r: Glycogen is converted to glucose, which is then used in respiration.
mistakes.w: Muscles use up glycogen as the energy source directly.

mistakes.r: It is made during exercise when oxygen supply is insufficient; the oxygen debt is repaid afterwards.
mistakes.w: Lactic acid is made when you stop exercising.

mistakes.r: It increases to supply more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide, because respiration rate has increased.
mistakes.w: Breathing rate increases because the body needs energy.

mistakes.r: It does release energy, but much less than aerobic respiration.
It is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to react with lactic acid and remove it.
mistakes.w: Oxygen debt is when the body runs out of oxygen.

mistakes.r: Heart rate goes up so blood carries oxygen and glucose to muscles faster and removes carbon dioxide faster.
mistakes.w: Heart rate goes up so oxygen is made.

mistakes.r: It is carried by the blood to the liver and converted back to glucose.
mistakes.w: Lactic acid is broken down in the muscles.

summary: AQA 4.4.2 asks you to describe and explain how heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume change during exercise, the role of glycogen, what happens when oxygen supply is insufficient (anaerobic respiration, lactic acid, fatigue) and how the oxygen debt is repaid. It matters because it links respiration, circulation, breathing and the liver in one commonly tested sequence.

terms.d: Respiration using oxygen to break down glucose completely, releasing energy; produces carbon dioxide and water.
Respiration without oxygen; in animals glucose is incompletely broken down to lactic acid, releasing much less energy.
The product of anaerobic respiration in animal (muscle) cells.
The amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.
Muscles become tired and stop contracting efficiently, often after long periods of vigorous activity.
A storage carbohydrate made of glucose, stored in the liver and muscles, converted back to glucose when needed.
The number of heart beats per minute.
The number of breaths taken per minute.
The volume of air taken in with each breath.
An exothermic reaction in cells that transfers energy from glucose.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings.
Partial breakdown of glucose, as in anaerobic respiration, so less energy is released.
The time taken for heart rate or breathing rate to return to resting levels after exercise.
Sub-cellular structures where most aerobic respiration reactions occur.

worked.q: A student's pulse was 70 beats per minute at rest and 154 beats per minute during exercise. Calculate the percentage increase. (2 marks)

worked.ans: Anaerobic respiration during the race produced lactic acid. After the race, extra oxygen is needed to react with the lactic acid and remove it (the oxygen debt), so breathing rate and heart rate stay high until the lactic acid has been converted back to glucose in the liver.
worked.q: Explain why a sprinter keeps breathing heavily after the race has finished. (4 marks)
steps: During the sprint, the oxygen supply was insufficient so the muscles respired anaerobically.
After the race extra oxygen is needed to react with the lactic acid (oxygen debt).
Lactic acid is carried by the blood to the liver and converted to glucose, so heart and breathing rates stay high.

worked.ans: A full-mark answer states: increased heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume with the reason (more oxygen and glucose to muscles, carbon dioxide removed); glycogen converted to glucose; anaerobic respiration glucose → lactic acid when oxygen is insufficient; muscle fatigue; oxygen debt repaid after exercise; lactic acid transported to the liver and converted to glucose.
worked.q: Describe and explain the changes in the body during exercise. (6 marks)
steps: Muscles contract more, so respiration rate increases to release more energy.
Heart rate increases to deliver oxygen and glucose faster and remove carbon dioxide.
Breathing rate and breath volume increase to take in more oxygen and remove CO2.
If oxygen is insufficient, anaerobic respiration occurs, forming lactic acid and causing fatigue.
Oxygen debt is repaid afterwards and lactic acid goes to the liver.
